— Senior Armed Forces commanders met with Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran's Supreme Commander-in-Chief.
During the meeting, the Supreme Leader issued several directives concerning potential threats and any renewed US-Israeli attacks:
• Every level and type of threat must be met with an immediate and effective response, without geographical limitations.
• The target bank must be updated to include all tangible and intangible assets belonging to the US and Israel within the reach of Iranian Armed Forces.
• If the US and Israel launch renewed military or terrorist attacks, Iran's Armed Forces and people will determine when and under what conditions they end.
• Strengthen military intelligence capabilities, deepen indigenous defense capabilities in both doctrine and tactics, and develop modern defense and security systems through the use of advanced technologies.
Senior Iranian military commanders also briefed Khamenei on the readiness of forces along the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman, and the country's northwestern and southeastern borders.
They also reported a several-fold increase in the production of ammunition and various reconnaissance, support, and combat weapons.

— A satellite image shows the aftermath of a Ukrainian strike using Long Neptune extended-range cruise missiles on Marinovka Air Base in Volgograd Oblast.
Burn marks are visible at two open aircraft parking areas following the strikes. The Ukrainian Navy says two Su-34 fighter-bombers were stationed there, although it is impossible to determine what exactly was destroyed based on the imagery alone. Several previously constructed aircraft shelters and protective hangars can also be seen nearby.
This is the fourth Ukrainian strike against Russian Aerospace Forces (VKS) air bases since the beginning of October, and the third to successfully hit its targets. Previous strikes damaged aircraft at Khanskaya and Borisoglebsk air bases, while the missiles launched at Baltimore Air Base failed to reach their targets.

— The U.S. State Department has approved a $2.1 billion sale of 500 PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) interceptors for Ukraine's Patriot air defense systems.
The purchase will be funded by Canada, Germany, Norway, and Ukrainian funds backed by the European Union. Lockheed Martin will be the main contractor.
However, the missiles have yet to be manufactured. With the U.S.-Iran war ongoing, Lockheed Martin's production capacity is likely to be focused first on meeting U.S. military requirements rather than supplying Ukraine.
No delivery timeline has been announced.
